newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan to see little inflationary pressure.
newsitem.headline: Japan to see little inflationary pressure.

text.p: Japan should see negligible inflationary pressure over the next business year, providing little justification for a credit tightening, economists predicted in a Reuters poll released on Thursday.
Economists said Japan was just coming out of a deflationary period and that any move by the central bank to raise the nation's ultra-low interest rates would not be due to inflation.
"Inflation is the least of the central bank's worries and can expect to be for some time," said Russell Jones, chief economist at Lehman Brothers Japan.
The Bank of Japan has kept the official discount rate at 0.5 percent since September 1995.

Predictions gathered from 30 economists produced a mean average forecast of a 1.6 percent rise in consumer prices for fiscal 1997/98, most of which they attributed to a rise in the sales tax to five percent from three percent on April 1.

Pressure was expected to remain slight over the next business year as well, with a mean average forecast of a 0.9 percent rise for fiscal 1998/99. That average was derived from a total of 18 forecasts.
The survey covered 33 brokerages and research bodies, although not all those polled responded to all the questions.
Although very little was seen dripping through to consumer prices, prices at the factory gate were expected to rise as import prices increase on the back of a weaker yen.
Economists said it would be difficult for firms to pass on the higher costs.

"Not only are Japanese firms facing more competition between themselves but they are also still facing pressure from cheaper overseas imports," said Junji Ota, research supervisor at Okasan Research Institute,
Twenty-five economists gave forecasts for wholesale price figures, producing a mean average rise of 1.7 percent in fiscal 1997/98 and 0.1 percent the next business year.
